units.title: Weather and Climate
units.intro:
Atmosphere layers (troposphere = weather kitchen). Weather = short-term state. Climate = long-term average. Elements: temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, clouds, precipitation.

Temperature: latitude, altitude (~6.5 °C / 1000 m), land/sea, clouds, ocean currents. Pressure: high = sinking dry; low = rising rain. Wind blows from high to low pressure; named from where it comes. Belts: trades, westerlies, polar. ITCZ = meeting of trades, rain. Precipitation: rain, snow, hail — convectional, orographic, frontal.

cards.title: 3.1 The Atmosphere
body: **The troposphere** is the lowest layer of the atmosphere found near the earth’s surface.
The atmosphere is useful to people because people and animals breathe the oxygen in it.
**Weather** is the condition of the atmosphere in a particular place over a short period of time.
**Meteorology** is the study of weather and a Meteorologist is the scientist who studies weather.

cards.problem: Which layer of the atmosphere contains over 75% of the total air mass and is the zone where almost all weather changes occur?

steps.text: **Step 1: Check the definitions of atmospheric layers.**
The Troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, extending up to $10 - 16\text{ km}$ from the Earth's surface.
It holds more than $75\%\text{ of the atmosphere's mass}$ and is the zone where clouds, rain, wind, and daily weather changes occur.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays from the Sun, is located within the:

steps.text: The ozone layer ($O_3$) is situated in the upper part of the second atmospheric layer.
This second layer, located directly above the Troposphere, is the Stratosphere.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Nitrogen and Oxygen together account for approximately what percentage of the total volume of the atmosphere?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the gas concentrations in the atmosphere.**
- Nitrogen ($N_2$): $78\%$
- Oxygen ($O_2$): $21\%$

**Step 2: Sum the percentages.**
$$\text{Total} = 78\% + 21\% = 99\%$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Together they account for **99%** of the atmospheric volume.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A scientist who studies long-term weather averages recorded over at least 30 years is a:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Differentiate between weather and climate studies.**
- Meteorology: short-term weather studies.
- Climatology: long-term weather averages over decades ($30+\text{ years}$).

**Step 2: Match with the scientist's title.**
A scientist specializing in climatology is a Climatologist.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct term is **Climatologist**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays from the Sun, is located within the:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Locate the ozone layer.**
The ozone layer ($O_3$) is situated in the upper part of the second atmospheric layer.

**Step 2: Identify the second layer.**
This second layer, located directly above the Troposphere, is the Stratosphere.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the ozone layer is located within the **Stratosphere**.

cards.title: 3.2 Relationship between Weather and Climate
body: Climate, on the other hand, is the average weather condition of an area during a long period of time.
**Climatology** is the study of climate and Climatologists are scientists who study climate.
To determine the climate of an area, they study the daily weather conditions over many years.
In most parts of Eritrea farmers grow crops in summer because it is a rainy season.

cards.title: Step by step: Weather and climate
body: **Step 1:** Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place at a particular time (hours or days).
**Step 2:** Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually at least 30 years.
**Step 3:** Both are described by the same elements: temperature, rainfall (precipitation), humidity, air pressure, wind, cloud and sunshine.
**Step 4:** Weather is studied by meteorology and recorded at weather stations; climate is studied by climatology using long records of those observations.
**Step 5:** So the link is: climate is built from many years of weather records.
**Example:** "It is raining heavily in Asmara this afternoon" describes weather. "Asmara gets most of its rain in July and August and has mild temperatures all year" describes climate.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Weather = Today, Climate = Thirty years
Exam tip
body: Look for time words in the question. "Today, this week, yesterday" → weather. "Usually, average, every year, for many years" → climate.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What percentage of the incoming solar radiation successfully enters the atmosphere and reaches the Earth's surface?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check the solar radiation partition values.**
Of the solar radiation entering the atmosphere, $19\%\text{ is absorbed}$ and $34\%\text{ is reflected/scattered}$.

**Step 2: Identify the percentage reaching the ground.**
Only **47%** of incoming solar radiation reaches the Earth's surface.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct percentage is **47%**.

cards.title: 3.3 Elements of weather and climate
body: The condition of these elements changes from place to place and even in the same place from time to time.
**Air temperature** is the measure of the hotness or coldness of air.
**The sun** is the source of all heat energy.
The heat energy radiated by the sun is called solar radiation or radiant energy while the part of that radiation that reaches the earth’s surface is known as **insolation**.

- Isobars: lines of equal pressure.
- Isohyets: lines of equal rainfall.
- Isotherms: lines of equal temperature.

**Step 2: Identify the correct term.**
Isotherms connect places of equal temperature.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct term is **Isotherms**.

cards.why: The pairing in option C is incorrect. **Humidity** is measured using a **Hygrometer** or a Psychrometer. A **weather vane** (or wind vane) is used to measure **wind direction**, not humidity.

cards.title: 3.4 Air Temperature
body: The transfer of heat from one object to another by contact is called **conduction**.
Since air is in contact with the earth’s surface, heat is transferred from the earth to the air molecules that are in contact with it by conduction.
In other words, temperature decreases when latitude increases.

cards.title: Formula
body: Lapse rate ≈ 6.5 °C cooler per 1000 m
Asmara vs Massawa: same tropical family, different height.

cards.title: Step by step: Air temperature
body: **Step 1:** The Sun heats the ground first (radiation); the ground then heats the air touching it (conduction), and warm air rises carrying heat upward (convection).
**Step 2:** Temperature is measured with a thermometer kept in a Stevenson screen, about 1.2 m above the ground, in the shade.
**Step 3:** Daily mean = (maximum + minimum) ÷ 2; daily range = maximum − minimum.
**Step 4:** Main controls: latitude (angle of the Sun), altitude (about 6.5 °C cooler per 1000 m), distance from the sea, ocean currents, aspect and cloud cover.
**Step 5:** Places of equal temperature are joined on maps by isotherms.
**Example:** Massawa (sea level) has a mean of about 30 °C. Asmara is about 2350 m higher: 2.35 × 6.5 ≈ 15 °C cooler, so about 15–17 °C – which matches Asmara's mild climate.

cards.title: Mnemonic — L-A-D-O-C
body: Latitude, Altitude, Distance from sea, Ocean currents, Cloud: the controls of temperature.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: In calculations always show the formula first: mean = (max + min) ÷ 2, range = max − min, cooling = height (km) × 6.5 °C. Write the unit °C with every answer.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The normal (environmental) lapse rate is about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m.

**Step 2:** Air is heated mainly from the ground, and thinner air holds less heat.

**Step 2:** The normal (environmental) lapse rate is about 6.5 °C per 1000 m.

**Step 3:** Answer: 6.5 °C per 1000 m.

**Tip:** Use it to compare Massawa and Asmara: about 2.35 km × 6.5 ≈ 15 °C difference.

cards.title: 3.5 Air Pressure
body: The density of air decreases upward with altitude.
Conclusion: When the cup is heated, the air inside it expands and then becomes light in weight.
Temperature has a great influence upon air pressure.
World Distribution of Air Pressure: Like temperature, air pressure is not the same everywhere.
The different rates of heating and cooling of land and sea also makes a big influence on the actual distribution of air pressure.

cards.title: Step by step: Air pressure
body: **Step 1:** Air pressure is the weight of the column of air pressing on a unit area of the Earth's surface.
**Step 2:** It is measured with a barometer (mercury or aneroid) in millibars (mb); average sea-level pressure is about 1013 mb.
**Step 3:** Pressure falls with height, because there is less air above you.
**Step 4:** Heated air expands, becomes lighter and rises → low pressure; cooled air contracts, becomes heavier and sinks → high pressure.
**Step 5:** Lines joining places of equal pressure are isobars; air always moves from high to low pressure, and that movement is wind.
**Example:** On a hot afternoon the land near Massawa heats quickly, air rises and pressure falls; the cooler Red Sea keeps higher pressure, so a sea breeze blows from the sea onto the land.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Hot air goes Higher → Low pressure; Cold air Collapses → High pressure ("hot-high-low, cold-down-high").
body: Hot air goes Higher → Low pressure; Cold air Collapses → High pressure ("hot-high-low, cold-down-high").

cards.title: Exam tip
body: For any wind question, first locate the high and the low – wind blows from high to low, and the closer the isobars, the stronger the wind.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which instrument is specifically used to measure wind speed at a weather station?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify meteorological instruments by function.**
- Wind Vane: measures wind direction.
- Barometer: measures pressure.
- Anemometer: measures wind speed.
- Hygrometer: measures humidity.

**Step 2: Select the matching instrument.**
The Anemometer is used to measure wind speed.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct instrument is the **Anemometer**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Saturated air is defined as air that has reached a Relative Humidity of:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define air saturation.**
Saturated air is holding the maximum possible amount of water vapor at its current temperature.

**Step 2: Convert to Relative Humidity.**
Because the actual moisture equals its maximum capacity, the ratio is $1.0$, which corresponds to **100% Relative Humidity**.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct percentage is **100%**.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A barometer measures atmospheric pressure (in millibars or hectopascals).

**Step 2:** A thermometer measures temperature; a rain gauge measures rainfall; a hygrometer measures humidity.

**Step 3:** So the answer is barometer.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: 3.6 Winds and Wind Belts
body: Demonstration: Principles of wind formation: Aim = to explain how wind is formed.
**The wind direction** is the direction from which the wind is blowing.
The doldrums (equatorial low) is an area of convergence (meeting) of winds.
The Northeast and Southeast trade winds originate from the horse latitudes (sub-tropical highs) around 300 N and 300S.
In general, it is the fastest along the equator and the slowest along the poles.

cards.title: Step by step: Winds and wind belts
body: **Step 1:** Wind is air moving horizontally from high to low pressure; it is named after the direction it comes from (a north wind blows from the north).
**Step 2:** Wind direction is shown by a wind vane; wind speed is measured with an anemometer.
**Step 3:** The Earth has pressure belts: equatorial low (doldrums), subtropical highs (about 30°N/S), subpolar lows (about 60°) and polar highs.
**Step 4:** Planetary winds blow between them: trade winds (30° → equator), westerlies (30° → 60°) and polar easterlies (poles → 60°).
**Step 5:** Rotation deflects them (Coriolis effect), so the north-east trades blow in the Northern Hemisphere and the south-east trades in the Southern.
**Example:** In Eritrea's lowlands in winter the north-east trade winds blow from the Arabian side towards the Red Sea coast and bring the coastal winter rains around Massawa.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Trade, West, East" from the equator to the pole
body: TWE: Trades, Westerlies, Easterlies.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When naming a wind, always say where it comes from, not where it goes. A wind blowing from the sea is an onshore (sea) wind.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the instrument used to measure the amount of water vapor (humidity) in the atmosphere?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify humidity measurement devices.**
The instrument used to measure relative humidity is the **Hygrometer**.

**Step 2: Confirm alternative instruments.**
- Thermometer: Temperature
- Barometer: Pressure
- Rain Gauge: Rainfall

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct instrument is the **Hygrometer**.

steps.text: The instrument used to measure relative humidity is the **Hygrometer**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which form of condensation is made up of ice crystals formed directly on window panes, grass, or the ground when temperatures drop below freezing?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check condensation forms below freezing.**
- Dew: liquid droplets, above freezing.
- Frost: solid ice crystals, below freezing.

**Step 2: Identify the correct match.**
Frost forms as ice crystals on cold ground surfaces when the dew point is below freezing.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct term is **Frost**.

steps.text: - Frost: solid ice crystals, below freezing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Trade winds originate from ___________ and blow to _________________.
cards.why: Trade winds are surface winds that blow from the **Sub-tropical High Pressure** belts (around $$ 30^\circ $$ N and S) toward the **Equatorial Low Pressure** belt (Doldrums).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The planetary winds that blow from the sub-tropical high-pressure belts (30 degrees N/S) toward the equatorial low-pressure belt (doldrums) are:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check global wind system paths.**
Winds blowing from $30^{\circ}\text{ N/S}$ (subtropical highs) to the equator ($0^{\circ}$, equatorial low) are the **Trade Winds**.

**Step 2: Verify the target destinations.**
This describes the North-East and South-East Trade Winds converging at the doldrums.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct winds are the **Trade Winds**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The planetary winds that blow from the sub-tropical high-pressure belts (30 degrees N/S) toward the equatorial low-pressure belt (doldrums) are:

steps.text: Winds blowing from $30^{\circ}\text{ N/S}$ (subtropical highs) to the equator ($0^{\circ}$, equatorial low) are the **Trade Winds**.
This describes the North-East and South-East Trade Winds converging at the doldrums.
Therefore, the correct winds are the **Trade Winds**.

cards.title: 3.7 Precipitation
body: The instrument that measures the amount of water vapour or humidity in the atmosphere is called **Hygrometer**.
Condensation and saturation: Condensation is the change of water vapour into liquid.
The temperature at which the point of saturation is reached is called **dew point**.
**Condensation** is the changing of water vapour back into drops of water.
Example: At 10 °C the amount of water vapour in the air is 9.41 grams per cubic meter; 10 °C is the dew point.

cards.title: Step by step: Precipitation
body: **Step 1:** Water evaporates and the air holds it as water vapour; humidity is measured with a hygrometer.
**Step 2:** When moist air rises it cools; at the dew point it becomes saturated and condensation forms clouds.
**Step 3:** When cloud droplets join and become too heavy, they fall as precipitation: rain, snow, sleet or hail.

**Step 4:** Three ways air is forced to rise give three types of rain: convectional (heating of the ground), relief or orographic (air forced over mountains) and frontal or cyclonic (warm air rising over cold air).
**Step 5:** Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge in millimetres; places of equal rainfall are joined by isohyets.

**Example:** Moist summer winds from the south-west are forced up the Eritrean escarpment and highlands; they cool, condense and give relief rain in July–August, while the leeward side stays drier (rain shadow).

cards.title: Mnemonic — C-R-F
body: Convection, Relief, Front: three ways to lift air, three types of rain.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: In a rain-type question, find the cause of the rising air: heat → convectional; a mountain → relief; meeting air masses → frontal.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If snow comes mixed with rain, because rain passes through a cold layer of the troposphere and freezes, it is called:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define precipitation varieties.**
- Sleet: snow mixed with rain.
- Hail: hard, ball-shaped ice formed during thunderstorms.

**Step 2: Match with the question's definition.**
Snow mixed with rain is defined as sleet.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct term is **Sleet**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: If snow comes mixed with rain, because rain passes through a cold layer of the troposphere and freezes, it is called:

steps.text: - Hail: hard, ball-shaped ice formed during thunderstorms.
Snow mixed with rain is defined as sleet.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the dry, sheltered side of a mountain that receives little or no rainfall called?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check the structure of orographic (relief) rainfall.**
Mountains have two sides: the windward side (wet, rising wind) and the leeward side (dry, descending wind).

**Step 2: Identify the term for the dry side.**
The dry side is called the leeward side or **Rain Shadow**.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the correct term is **Leeward or Rain Shadow side**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: What is the dry, sheltered side of a mountain that receives little or no rainfall called?

steps.text: **Step 1: Check the structure of orographic (relief) rainfall.**
Mountains have two sides: the windward side (wet, rising wind) and the leeward side (dry, descending wind).
**Step 2: Identify the term for the dry side.**
The dry side is called the leeward side or **Rain Shadow**.
Thus, the correct term is **Leeward or Rain Shadow side**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: __________ is a form of precipitation where snow comes mixed with the rain.
cards.why: Sleet occurs when snow melts as it falls through a warm layer of air and then refreezes into small ice pellets before hitting the ground, often appearing as a mix of rain and snow.

tips.text: In geography, when we speak about temperature we usually mean the hotness or coldness of the air around us. This heat is received by the atmosphere in different ways.
Air temperature varies from place to place. It also varies from time to time in the same place.
Several factors contribute to this variation in temperature.
Since air temperature has great effect on our daily life and activities, it is important for us to have the knowledge and skills of how to measure and record it.
The atmosphere of the earth extends upwards for several thousand kilometers. It is composed of different gases, dusts, moistures, smoke particles etc.
This force of pressing of gases and others from the top of the atmosphere down to the ground is called air pressure.
Air pressure is influenced by altitude and temperature the density of air decreases upwards with altitude.
When air is heated it expands and it becomes less in density than the surrounding air. So it ascends (ripse) This creates low pressure.

When air is cooled it contracts and becomes denser than the surrounding air. This creates pressing force on the ground that leads to high pressure. It varies from the equator to the poles and from land to sea.
Therefore, the same as air temperature, air pressure is not the same everywhere.

questions.answer: Hours–days vs decades of typical weather.
why: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place over hours or days; climate is the average weather pattern over a long period (about 30 years).
questions.label: 1. Weather vs climate?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: If we say 'Sawa is very hot', this refers to:  A) the weather  B) the slope  C) the climate  D) the land-use system  E) soil degradation
similar.a: C. the climate — Answer: C.

questions.answer: Weather happens — temperature generally falls with height.
why: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere (up to about 8–16 km); it contains almost all water vapour and clouds, and temperature falls with height.
questions.label: 2. Troposphere is where?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The weather forming process of the earth is greatly influenced by the layer of the atmosphere known as  A) Troposphere.  B) Stratosphere.  C) Mesosphere.  D) Thermosphere.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: A. Troposphere. — Answer: A.

questions.answer: Temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, cloud, precipitation.
why: The elements of weather and climate are temperature, air pressure, wind (speed and direction), humidity, cloud cover and precipitation.
questions.label: 3. Six elements (name four)?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Elements of weather and climate consist of  A) temperature.  B) precipitation.  C) humidity.  D) wind.  E) All of the above.
similar.a: E. All of the above. — All four listed are elements. Answer: E.

questions.answer: High sun angle, little seasonal slack.
why: Near the equator the noon Sun is always high in the sky, so its energy is concentrated on a small area and passes through less atmosphere; day length is about 12 hours all year.
questions.label: 4. Why equator is hot?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Why mountains are cooler?
similar.a: Lapse rate — thinner air, less heat kept.

questions.answer: Lapse rate — thinner air, less heat kept.
why: Temperature falls by about 6.5 °C per 1 000 m of height (lapse rate) because the air is thinner and is heated from the ground; Asmara (2 300 m) is much cooler than Massawa.
questions.label: 5. Why mountains are cooler?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The lapse rate of temperature can be defined as:  A) increase of temperature as altitude increases  B) decrease of temperature as altitude decreases  C) increase of temperature as altitude decreases  D) increase in density of air upward with altitude  E) decrease in density of air downward with altitude
similar.a: C. increase of temperature as altitude decreases — Answer: C.

questions.answer: Land heats and cools fast — bigger range inland.
why: Land heats up and cools down faster than water, so places far from the sea have hotter summers, colder winters and a larger temperature range.
questions.label: 6. Continentality?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Sea breeze day idea?
similar.a: Land hotter → low pressure over land → wind off the sea.

questions.answer: Land hotter → low pressure over land → wind off the sea.
why: By day the land heats faster than the sea; air over the land rises (low pressure) and cooler air from the sea (higher pressure) blows in as a sea breeze.
questions.label: 7. Sea breeze day idea?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: A wind that blows from the floor of a valley to the mountain slope is called  A) sea breeze.  B) land breeze.  C) mountain breeze.  D) anabatic wind.  E) katabatic wind.
similar.a: D. anabatic wind. — At night cold air drains downslope – the mountain breeze or katabatic wind. Answer: D.

questions.answer: Sinking air, often clear and dry.
why: In a high-pressure area air sinks and warms, so clouds do not form; the weather is usually clear, dry and calm.
questions.label: 8. High pressure weather?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: When air is heated, it expands, becomes less dense and rises up. Such a process is responsible for the formation of  A) low pressure area.  B) high pressure area.  C) tropical high pressure area.  D) sub-tropical high pressure area.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: A. low pressure area. — Answer: A.

questions.answer: Rising air, clouds, rain likely.
why: In a low-pressure area air rises and cools; water vapour condenses into clouds, and rain is likely.
questions.label: 9. Low pressure weather?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: A steep gradient of isobars indicates that the  A) speed of the wind is high.  B) speed of the wind is low.  C) difference in air pressure between two places is high.  D) difference in air pressure between two places is low.  E) A and C.
similar.a: E. A and C. — Both A and C are true. Answer: E.

questions.answer: The direction it comes from.
why: Winds are named after the direction they blow from: a north wind blows from the north towards the south.
questions.label: 10. Wind is named from?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An anemometer is an instrument used to measure the ______ of a place.  A) temperature  B) rainfall  C) pressure  D) wind speed  E) wind direction
similar.a: D. wind speed — Temperature – thermometer; rainfall – rain gauge; pressure – barometer; wind direction – wind vane. Answer: D.

questions.answer: Blow toward the ITCZ from the subtropical highs.
why: Trade winds blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts (about 30°N and S) towards the equatorial low (ITCZ), turned by the Earth's rotation into north-east and south-east trades.
questions.label: 11. Trade winds?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Winds that originate from the sub-tropical high pressure and blow toward the doldrums are called the  A) Trade Winds.  B) Westerly Winds.  C) Monsoon Winds.  D) Polar Easterlies.  E) Polar Westerlies.
similar.a: A. Trade Winds. — The westerlies blow from the sub-tropical highs towards the sub-polar lows. Answer: A.

questions.answer: Inter-tropical convergence — rising air, heavy rain.
why: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is where the trade winds meet near the equator; the warm air rises strongly, forming tall clouds and heavy rain.
questions.label: 12. ITCZ?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An instrument used to measure the relative humidity of air is called  A) anemometer.  B) barometer.  C) thermometer.  D) hygrometer.  E) rain gauge.
similar.a: D. hygrometer. — Anemometer = wind speed; barometer = pressure; rain gauge = rainfall. Answer: D.

questions.answer: Air forced up a mountain, cools, rains on the windward side.
why: When moist air is forced to rise over a mountain it cools, water vapour condenses and rain falls on the windward side — orographic (relief) rain.
questions.label: 13. Orographic rain?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The type of rainfall formed when moisture-laden wind is forced to rise over high ground is  A) conventional.  B) cyclonic.  C) orographic.  D) relief.  E) C and D.
similar.a: E. C and D. — Orographic and relief rainfall are two names for the same thing, so both C and D are right. Answer: E.

questions.answer: Dry leeward side.
why: After crossing the mountain the air descends on the leeward side, warms and becomes drier, so little rain falls there — the rain shadow.
questions.label: 14. Rain shadow?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The speed of wind is measured by:  A) Barometer  B) Hygrometer  C) Rain gauge  D) Wind vane  E) Anemometer
similar.a: E. Anemometer — Answer: E.

questions.answer: Hot ground heats air; it rises and rains (tropics, afternoons).
why: Strong heating of the ground warms the air above it; the air rises, cools and forms cumulonimbus clouds, giving heavy afternoon showers, often with thunder.
questions.label: 15. Convectional rain?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An equipment used to measure air pressure is  A) an anemometer.  B) a barometer.  C) a hygrometer.  D) a thermometer.  E) a rain gauge.
similar.a: B. a barometer. — Anemometer = wind speed; hygrometer = humidity; thermometer = temperature; rain gauge = rainfall. Answer: B.

questions.answer: Warm and cold air masses meet; warm air is lifted.
why: When a warm and a cold air mass meet at a front, the lighter warm air is lifted over the denser cold air, cools and gives frontal rain.
questions.label: 16. Frontal rain?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: A type of rainfall formed when warm air and cold air converge is  A) Conventional.  B) Orographic.  C) Frontal.  D) Relief.  E) B and D.
similar.a: C. Frontal. — Orographic (= relief) rain forms when air is forced up a mountain; convectional rain forms when heated air rises. Answer: C.

questions.answer: Water vapour in the air.
why: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; relative humidity compares it with the maximum the air could hold at that temperature (as a percentage).
questions.label: 17. Humidity is?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: At −15 °C a mass of air holds 1.62 grams of water vapour per cubic metre, while at 10 °C it holds 9.41 grams of water vapour per cubic metre. This implies that the capacity of air to hold moisture  A) decreases when temperature increases.  B) increases when temperature decreases.  C) increases when temperature increases.  D) remains constant at any given time.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: C. increases when temperature increases. — Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. So capacity increases as temperature increases. Answer: C.

questions.answer: Temperature at which air becomes saturated — dew or cloud can form.
why: The dew point is the temperature at which air, if cooled, becomes saturated; further cooling causes condensation as dew, fog or cloud.
questions.label: 18. Dew point flavour?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The temperature at which air becomes saturated is the  A) boiling point.  B) melting point.  C) freezing point.  D) dew point.  E) sublimation point.
similar.a: D. dew point. — Answer: D.

questions.answer: Line of equal pressure on a map.
why: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining places with the same air pressure (reduced to sea level).
questions.label: 19. Isobar?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Isohyet is an imaginary line drawn on a map that shows the distribution of  A) temperature.  B) pressure.  C) rainfall.  D) sunshine.  E) volcanoes.
similar.a: C. rainfall. — Isotherms show temperature, isobars pressure, isohels sunshine. Answer: C.

questions.answer: Strong pressure gradient → strong wind.
why: Closely spaced isobars mean pressure changes quickly over a short distance (steep pressure gradient), so winds are strong.
questions.label: 20. Close isobars mean?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Imaginary lines drawn on a map joining places of equal atmospheric pressure are  A) isohyets.  B) isobars.  C) isopleths.  D) isotherms.  E) isochrones.
similar.a: B. isobars. — Answer: B.

questions.answer: Temperature.
why: A thermometer measures air temperature; maximum and minimum thermometers record the highest and lowest temperatures of the day.
questions.label: 21. Thermometer measures?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: What is the average daily temperature of a place if the daily maximum and minimum are 42.3 °C and 21.8 °C?  A) 64.1 °C  B) 32.05 °C  C) 20.5 °C  D) 5.3 °C  E) 2.1 °C
similar.a: B. 32.05 °C — Answer: B. (20.5 °C is the daily RANGE; 64.1 °C is just the sum.)

questions.answer: Rainfall depth.
why: A rain gauge collects rain falling on a known area; the depth of water collected (in mm) is the rainfall.
questions.label: 22. Rain gauge measures?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An instrument used to measure the speed of wind is called  A) anemometer.  B) barometer.  C) hygrometer.  D) rain gauge.  E) thermometer.
similar.a: A. anemometer. — Barometer = air pressure; hygrometer = humidity; rain gauge = rainfall; thermometer = temperature. Answer: A.

questions.answer: Subtropical highs — sinking air.
why: Air rising at the equator descends around 30°N and S; sinking air warms and dries, creating subtropical high pressure and deserts such as the Sahara.
questions.label: 23. Why deserts at ~30°?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An instrument used to measure the amount of water vapor in the air is  A) hygrometer.  B) barometer.  C) thermometer.  D) rain gauge.  E) wind vane.
similar.a: A. hygrometer. — A barometer measures air pressure, a thermometer temperature, a rain gauge rainfall and a wind vane wind direction. Answer: A.

questions.answer: Cumuliform = heap/convection. Stratiform = layer.
why: Cumulus (heap) clouds form from rising currents of air (convection); stratus (layer) clouds form when a wide layer of air is cooled gently.
questions.label: 24. Cloud type flavour?

similar.q: Evaporation vs condensation?
similar.a: Liquid→vapour vs vapour→liquid (needs cooling or a surface).

questions.answer: Liquid→vapour vs vapour→liquid (needs cooling or a surface).
why: Evaporation is liquid water changing to water vapour (needs heat); condensation is water vapour changing back to liquid when air is cooled to its dew point.
questions.label: 25. Evaporation vs condensation?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The process by which water changes from liquid to solid state is  A) condensation.  B) evaporation.  C) evapo-transpiration.  D) sublimation.  E) freezing.
similar.a: E. freezing. — Condensation is gas → liquid, evaporation liquid → gas, sublimation solid → gas directly. Answer: E.

questions.answer: Evaporate, condense, precipitate (plus runoff).
why: Water evaporates from seas and land, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation and returns to the sea by run-off and groundwater — the water (hydrological) cycle.

why: Eritrea is in the tropics, but the high altitude of the highlands lowers temperatures (lapse rate), giving Asmara a mild climate.

similar.q: Changes in weather and climate are due to  A) latitude.  B) altitude.  C) ocean currents.  D) distance from the sea.  E) All of the above.

questions.answer: ITCZ follows the overhead sun — rain belts move.
why: The ITCZ follows the overhead Sun: it moves north in June–August (bringing summer rain to the Eritrean highlands) and south in December–February.

similar.a: A. meters per second. — Both A and D are common units, so both are accepted. Keyed A; D also accepted.
